newsitem.title: HUNGARY: DERIVATIVES SEEN BROADENING CESI'S APPEAL.
newsitem.headline: DERIVATIVES SEEN BROADENING CESI'S APPEAL.

text.p: The Central European Share Index (CESI), now one year old, is a good indicator for investors in the region but market players believe it will better fulfil its role once the Budapest Stock Exchange (BSE) offers derivatives on it.

The CESI index, which is calculated in dollar terms, currently reflects price movements of 73 selected Polish, Czech, Hungarian, Slovak and Slovenian stocks and celebrates its first birthday on February 1.
"Once futures contracts are available on the CESI, it will be an ideal product for fund managers who invest in central Europe," a Budapest-based trader said.

He was knocking on an open door as far as the BSE's CEO Jozsef Rotyis was concerned. Rotyis said recently the bourse was considering launching futures for the CESI but a number of issues were still to be solved.
"(Regarding the CESI futures) a number of questions, such as the choice between dollar or forint quotation, are yet to be answered," Rotyis told Reuters last week.
Nevertheless, the index, already suits some, even in its current form.
"I use the CESI as a reference point -- it's actually quite useful," said Lubomir Vystavel, an equities dealer at ING Barings in Prague.

"(The CESI's usefulness) depends on who the information is for -- if it's for a fund generally active in Central Europe then it certainly provides a picture of the whole region," said Tomasz Cwintal, an analyst at Bank Gospodarki Zywnosciowej (BGZ) brokerage.
"But if it's for investors who want to invest in individual markets then the indices of the individual bourses are better."
Currently 24 Polish stocks are in the index but some believe the Warsaw market should be better reflected.
"Ever more firms are entering the Polish bourse and its capitalisation is increasing at a greater rate than that of other bourses in the region...," BGZ's Cwintal said.
The Warsaw's market capitalisation grew by 113 percent in zloty terms in 1996 to 24 billion zlotys (which is $8.3 billion) at the exchange rate at the turn of this year.

"The capitalisation of the Polish bourse could increase by 40 percent by the end of the year if privatisations of large firms such as Polska Miedz and Bank Handlowy take place," he said, referring to copper giant KGHM Polska Miedz SA and Bank Handlowy SA.

Only the Budapest bourse outperformed Warsaw in the CESI countries in terms of equity capitalisation growth last year, surging to 852.46 billion forints ($5 billion) at the end of 1996 from 327.78 billion forints a year before.
On December 31, the CESI basket had a capitalisation of $22 billion compared and represented 71.37 percent of the total capitalisation of the official equity markets.
Vystavel noted, however, that the CESI did not always seem to correlate with movements on national bourses.
"It's quite interesting sometimes that you can see all the regional (national) indices are down but the CESI is up," he said.

An opposite move by the CESI from the national indices is quite rare -- the CESI's correlation with the main indices of the Budapest, Warsaw and Prague exchanges is above 0.95 -- but disparities can happen when one or more of the bourses are closed, a bourse source told Reuters.
On such occasions dollar exchange rate changes can substantially influence the index, she explained.
